Formal tone: A formal tone is common in a professional contexts. This tone focuses on being thorough and direct yet respectful. It uses complete words rather than contractions and emphasizes facts and grammatical correctness.

Informal tone: An informal tone is the opposite of a formal tone. Informal tone is conversational and expressive, similar to how people would speak to a friend. It uses contractions, colloquial phrases, and more emotion than formal writing. Its sentence structure can be shorter and feature a choppy rhythm, or it can be long and chatty.
Optimistic tone: An optimistic tone can convey a sense of hope and a positive outlook for the future. It uses uplifting language to express satisfaction and aspiration.
Worried tone: A worried tone can make reader apprehensive or uneasy. It communicates feelings of anxiousness about something unknown.

Friendly tone: A friendly tone is warm, nonthreatening, and can elicit trust. This tone can also have a mix of formal or informal tones. Generally, it’s lighthearted and kind. Exclamation points can convey warmth or enthusiasm.
Curious tone: A curious tone tells the reader that there are compelling details that you still want to uncover. Use this tone creatively to keep your reader intrigued about learning more.
Assertive tone: An assertive tone exudes confidence and authority. It can also be insistent and straightforward. This tone can help you persuade your audience about a topic.
Encouraging tone: An encouraging tone is supportive and understanding. It gives readers reassurance to overcome their fears and take action.
Surprised tone: When writing with a surprised tone, you capture how something is unexpected. This tone can elicit different types of astonishment, such as joy or shock.

Cooperative tone: A cooperative tone is typical in the workplace. Your word choice—often evoking positivity and collaboration—and use of the pronoun we can invite mutual participation toward a shared goal.
